q: The neurotransmitter released by photoreceptors to signal the next neuron is:
w: Photoreceptors release glutamate, most heavily in the dark. Light reduces its release. Dopamine and GABA act elsewhere in the retina.

q: In response to light, the photoreceptor membrane undergoes:
w: Light closes cGMP-gated sodium channels, so the cell hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate, unlike a typical neuron that depolarizes.

q: The second messenger broken down by the enzyme phosphodiesterase in phototransduction is:
w: Activated phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cGMP, dropping its level so the sodium channels close. cAMP and IP3 are messengers in other pathways.

q: The enzyme that regenerates 11-cis retinal from all-trans retinal is:
w: Retinal isomerase (in the visual cycle) converts all-trans retinal back to 11-cis retinal to reform rhodopsin. The others regulate the cascade.

q: The retinal layer that receives the greatest blood supply from the choriocapillaris is the:
w: The choriocapillaris nourishes the outer retina, including the photoreceptors and RPE. The inner retina is supplied by the central retinal artery.

q: The largest ganglion cells, which also conduct fastest, are the:
w: Y (magnocellular, parasol) cells are large and fast, carrying motion and low-contrast information. X (parvocellular, midget) cells are smaller and slower.

q: Regarding longitudinal chromatic aberration of the eye, which is true?
o: red light has a shorter focal length than blue
all wavelengths focus at the same point
green light focuses in front of blue
ans: blue light has a shorter focal length than red
w: Short-wavelength blue light refracts more, so it has a shorter focal length and focuses in front of red. This is longitudinal chromatic aberration.
k: Blue bends most, focuses first (shortest focal length).

q: Depth of focus of the eye is increased by:
w: A smaller pupil narrows the cone of light and increases depth of focus and depth of field, the pinhole effect.
k: Small pupil = more depth of focus.

q: The most important factor determining retinal image size is:
w: Axial length is the dominant factor in retinal image size; a longer eye gives a larger image. Optical powers matter less than the eye's length.
k: Retinal image size is set mainly by axial length.

q: Compared with parvocellular neurons, magnocellular neurons are:
w: Magnocellular neurons respond to motion and low contrast and conduct quickly, but are colorblind and low-resolution. Parvocellular neurons carry detail and color.
k: Magno = low contrast and motion; parvo = detail and color.

q: Which ultraviolet band penetrates deepest into skin and ocular tissues?
w: UV-A has the longest ultraviolet wavelength, so it penetrates deepest. UV-B and UV-C are shorter and absorbed more superficially.
k: UV-A is longest, so it goes deepest.

q: A lesion of the right optic radiation produces:
w: Retrochiasmal lesions cause a homonymous defect on the opposite side, so a right radiation lesion gives a left homonymous hemianopsia.

q: A fixed, dilated, usually unilateral pupil caused by central nervous system compression is called:
w: Hutchinson's pupil is a fixed, dilated, usually unilateral pupil from third-nerve compression, as in uncal herniation. The others are different pupil signs.
k: Fixed dilated pupil from compression = Hutchinson.

q: A patient who can fuse images but cannot appreciate depth has which grade of binocular vision?
w: Grade II is fusion without stereopsis. Grade I is simultaneous perception, and Grade III adds stereopsis (depth).
k: Fuse but no depth = Grade II.

q: A patient who passes all nine sets of the Titmus circles demonstrates a stereoacuity of:
w: Passing all nine Titmus circle sets corresponds to 40 seconds of arc, the finest level on that test.

q: In the red-lens test, a patient who sees a single pink light has:
w: Seeing one pink light means the red and white images have merged, indicating fusion. Two separate lights would mean diplopia, and one color means suppression.
